problem: Transformer-based VLN agents (e.g. RecBERT, HAMT) entangle orientation (spatial) and visual (landmark) information in one representation, limiting what each source contributes. Their pre-training tasks are also generic and not designed for the downstream model.
motivation: Some instructions can be solved with orientation cues alone ("turn left 90 degrees") and others with landmark recognition alone ("walk to the sofa"). Separating the two abilities, and pre-training each specifically, should let the agent ground each cue more effectively.
key_idea: Add explicit orientation and vision modules alongside the history module in a recurrent VLN Transformer, fuse their action scores, and pre-train each module with dedicated Orientation Matching and Vision Matching tasks.
insight: Modular design plus matching pre-training helps: the pre-training alone lifts RecBERT (unseen SR 0.61 to 0.63), and LOViS on top adds a further gain (0.65). In the module ablation, H+V gives unseen SR 0.642 and H+O gives 0.629, so vision matters more than orientation, and all three together give the best 0.653. VM and OM help little separately in unseen environments but help together (LOViS unseen SR 0.653 with both vs 0.649 for MLM+SSAP), with larger gains in seen environments.
method: History module: RecBERT-style recurrent state; cross-attention between text and [state; vision+orientation] features, then self-attention. This is the only module that updates the state, and it outputs score p^h.
Orientation module: linearly projects the 128-d heading/elevation features, applies cross-attention with text and its own state (State-O), then self-attention, giving orientation-only score p^o.
Vision module: projects ResNet-152 2048-d features of navigable viewpoints, applies cross-attention with text and its own state (State-V), then self-attention, giving vision-only score p^v.
Action selection: concatenates [p^h; p^o; p^v] and applies a learned linear layer W_a and softmax over candidate viewpoints. Training mixes IL and RL as in EnvDrop/RecBERT, with greedy inference.
Modified MLM: masks only direction tokens (from an R2R-derived dictionary) and landmark tokens (nouns by POS tag) with 8% probability, conditioned on orientation and vision features.
Modified SSAP: predicts the action from the cross-attention distribution of [CLS] over panorama images instead of a direct 36-way classifier.

Vision Matching (VM) and Orientation Matching (OM): VM is binary matching of instruction to vision-only features with negatives from other environments. OM predicts the 4-d heading/elevation orientation feature from the instruction and the initial orientation. Pre-training initializes from PREVALENT weights.

setting.backbone: PREVALENT-initialized BERT-style language Transformer (9 layers) plus cross-modal Transformer (4 layers), with ResNet-152 image features; trained
setting.training_data: R2R train instruction-trajectory pairs plus the RecBERT augmented data (PREVALENT-style image-text-action triplets) for pre-training, then fine-tuning with IL+RL for 30k iterations; also trained on R4R
setting.observation: Navigable-viewpoint views from the panorama, ResNet-152 features, plus relative heading/elevation

numbers.extra: single run; uses RecBERT augmented data
numbers.evidence: Table 1 row 13: NE 3.71, SR 0.65, SPL 0.59 val unseen

numbers_note: Values printed as fractions (e.g. 0.65) are converted to percentages; NE is in meters. The R4R table header mislabels NE with an up arrow.
results: On R2R, LOViS reaches val-unseen SR 65 / SPL 59 and test SR 63 / SPL 58, slightly above its reproduced RecBERT baseline (61/56 val unseen) and HAMT with ResNet-152 (64/58). On R4R val-unseen it improves over reproduced RecBERT: CLS 45 vs 41, sDTW 23 vs 21, SR 45 vs 43.
limitations: Gains over strong baselines are small (about 1-2 points SR on R2R unseen), and the results are single-run with no variance reported.
Evaluated only in discrete VLN (R2R/R4R) with ResNet-152 features. Newer ViT-based HAMT variants are not compared, and the modules are not tested in continuous environments.
The orientation and vision separation relies on heuristics (a direction dictionary, POS-tag nouns) and hand-designed negatives for pre-training.
